title: Will Iraq’s return to Jurf al-Sakhar weaken Iran-backed Kataib Hezbollah
author: Shelly Kittleson
text:
Analysis

Will Iraq’s return to Jurf al-Sakhar weaken Iran-backed Kataib Hezbollah

The town and surrounding agricultural area had been under the control of Iran-backed armed factions since 2014.

Shelly Kittleson

Iraqi soldiers deploy in Jurf al-Sakhar, the main stronghold of the Iran-backed Kataib Hezbollah, on Nov. 20 as Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi steps up efforts to rein in the faction.
— Ahmad Al-Rubaye / AFP via Getty Images

AMMAN – On Nov. 20, for the first time in more than a decade, forces answering to the Iraqi government entered Jurf al-Sakhar, an area south of Baghdad that even senior Iraqi officials had long said they could not tread.The previous day, Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi ordered the establishment of a joint security command under the federal police in the area, which the government referred to as Jurf al-Nasr in its announcement. Babil’s provincial council adopted that name after the area was recaptured from the Islamic State in 2014. Federal records still use Jurf al-Sakhar, the name displaced residents continue to use.The town and surrounding agricultural area had been under the control of Iran-backed armed factions since 2014 and became a stronghold of Kataib Hezbollah (KH). The Pentagon said in March 2020 that the group used sites in Jurf al-Sakhar to store heavy rockets and other weapons and to produce propellant. A 2021 analysis by the Washington Institute for Near East Policy said KH had repurposed some industrial sites in the area to produce, test and store rockets and explosives. Restricted access made other claims, including reports that non-Iraqi fighters trained there, difficult to corroborate.The new command will oversee units from the Iraqi army, federal police, Popular Mobilization Units (PMU) and energy police, Sabah al-Numan, spokesperson for the commander-in-chief of the armed forces, said in a Nov. 19 statement.
